instructions:
You are the resilience analyst of an AI-driven chaos-engineering agent. The system under test is Google's Online
Boutique (11 gRPC microservices) on single-node Kubernetes. You get the measured facts of every experiment, the
dependency map, the baseline, the planner's predictions and how they held, anchor scores computed by code, and the
catalog of fixes.

Produce:
1. Findings = weaknesses, ranked by severity (most severe first). Severity scale: {"critical": "users cannot shop or check out (outage or most requests failing) and nothing contains it", "high": "a core flow (product, cart, checkout) breaks or becomes unusably slow (seconds), or recovery is slow", "medium": "noticeable degradation with a workaround or limited scope (one flow, moderate slowdown)", "low": "minor impact, or a configuration weakness without measured user impact yet"}.
   Each finding: affected services, the run ids that show it (exactly as given), the measured numbers, the root
   cause (explain the mechanism, e.g. sequential calls without deadlines amplify latency), ONE fix from the fix
   catalog with concrete parameters, why it addresses the root cause, the improvement you expect, and the
   experiment to re-run after the fix (same type/target/params as the evidence run when possible).
   Positive findings (e.g. graceful degradation) may be included as low severity with a code_change or posture fix
   only if useful; do not invent problems without evidence. Merge findings that share one root cause.
2. Resilience scores: for EVERY service in the anchors table, score each rubric dimension 0-100:
   {"availability": "Did users keep getting successful responses? 100 = no extra errors; 70 = a few % errors or short error bursts; 40 = sustained errors on some flows; 0 = most requests failed.", "latency": "How much slower did user flows get (worst p95 vs baseline)? 100 = < 1.5x; 80 = ~3x; 60 = ~10x; 30 = ~50x; 0 = several seconds / timeouts.", "recovery": "How fast were users back to normal after the fault ended? 100 = immediately or never impacted; 75 = ~30 s; 50 = ~60 s; 0 = not recovered within 180 s.", "containment": "Did the failure stay contained? 100 = callers degraded gracefully, no spread; lower when flows that depend on the service broke, when unrelated flows/pods were hit, or when the guard had to stop the experiment.", "posture": "Static resilience configuration: 100 = >= 2 replicas, readiness + liveness probes, CPU/memory limits; single replica -40, missing readiness -20, missing liveness -10, missing limits -20."}
   Start from the anchor and stay within +-15 of it; deviate only with a reason (e.g. impact
   on an optional feature like ads matters less; a slow recovery on the checkout path matters more). Untested
   services: score availability/latency/recovery/containment from posture and dependencies, close to the anchor
   (anchors for untested dimensions are null - use your judgement and say so). Choose a criticality weight per
   service (0.5-3) reflecting business impact (checkout path and entrypoint high, ads/recommendations low).
3. Explain how you weighed services, review how well the planner's predictions held, and list limitations
   (single VM, small probe, short experiments).
Use only facts you are given or fetch with the tools. Answer only with the structured report.

output.summary: The cartservice pod kill caused broad, severe shopper impact: 90.48% impact error rate across all five flows, with the guard unable to stop the instantaneous fault and recovery taking 27.6 seconds. The paymentservice failure broke checkout for 75% of sampled checkout requests and coincided with a severe add-to-cart latency spike; the guard did abort that experiment. Both tested services are single replicas, making redundancy the clearest catalog fix. Confidence is limited by two short experiments and the small per-flow samples.

findings.title: Single cartservice replica outage disrupts every shopping flow
findings.evidence: The run reached a 100% peak error rate and 90.48% impact error rate; all five flows were affected. Per-flow error rates were home 87%, product 90.9%, add_to_cart 95%, view_cart 80%, and checkout 100%. The worst flow, view_cart, had p95 431.6 ms (28.21x its 15.3 ms baseline); peak p95 was 711.7 ms. Recovery took 27.6 s and the replacement pod became ready in 22.6 s. The guard reported an error-rate breach above 20% but did not abort the instantaneous pod kill.
findings.root_cause: cartservice has one replica and serves both frontend and checkoutservice across all five flows. Killing that sole instance leaves callers without a serving cartservice until Kubernetes replaces and readies a pod.
findings.fix_rationale: Adding replicas removes the tested single-instance failure mode for this stateless service, so a single pod kill should not take cart operations offline while replacement is underway.
findings.expected_improvement: With one replica killed, the remaining replicas should continue serving cart requests; error rates across the five flows should fall substantially, view_cart latency should be closer to baseline, and recovery should no longer depend on waiting for a replacement pod.

findings.title: Paymentservice failure breaks checkout and coincides with severe add-to-cart latency
findings.evidence: The run peaked at a 25% error rate and 729.2 ms p95 (110.48x the 6.6 ms add_to_cart baseline); the impact error rate was 15%. Checkout had a 75% flow error rate, while add_to_cart had 0% errors but p95 of 729.2 ms. The guard aborted the fault after 19.7 s when error rate exceeded 20%; recovery was reported as 1.0 s after the kill switch removed the fault.
findings.root_cause: paymentservice is a single replica on the revenue-critical checkout path, so its unavailability causes checkout requests to fail. The add_to_cart latency spike is also measured in this run, but the dependency map does not establish a direct paymentservice dependency for that flow, so its precise mechanism is uncertain.
findings.fix_rationale: paymentservice is stateless and has no redundancy. A second replica addresses the tested single-instance failure mode and should preserve payment availability when one pod is unavailable.
findings.expected_improvement: A single paymentservice pod failure should cause fewer checkout errors and reduce the checkout interruption that triggered the guard. Whether the observed add_to_cart latency spike also improves should be checked, since its mechanism is not established by the available dependency data.

For all untested services, availability, latency, recovery, and containment remain at 60 rather than treating dependency reach as measured failure behavior; their one-replica posture with probes and limits is also 60. Criticality weights reflect business impact and reach: frontend, cartservice, productcatalogservice, and redis-cart are highest, while emailservice, adservice, and recommendationservice are lower because their listed flow reach is narrower or their role is less directly revenue-critical. output.planner_review: The cartservice prediction was confirmed in 20261011-064201-pod_kill-cartservice: all five predicted flows were affected, the error and slowdown bands matched, and the run completed as predicted. The paymentservice prediction was partly confirmed in 20261011-064314-pod_failure-paymentservice: the run was aborted by the guard as predicted and checkout errors occurred, but the predicted absence of severe slowdown was wrong; measured peak p95 was 729.2 ms, a 110.48x factor, and add_to_cart was also listed among the affected flows. The latency miss shows that the planner did not anticipate this measured latency impact; the available data does not establish its exact mechanism.
limitations: The system runs on a single-node Kubernetes deployment, so results do not establish resilience to node or availability-zone failure.
Only two short experiments were run, covering pod_kill and pod_failure; most services and fault classes, including traffic spikes, network faults, CPU stress, and memory stress, were not tested.
Per-flow samples were small (roughly 16–23 requests in the reported runs), so error rates and p95 values may be noisy.
The missing shoppingassistantservice entry in the dependency map and the absence of direct tests for most services limit conclusions about the full dependency graph.
